title: Portland Colorado Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Portland well records show a 138 ft median depth, 12 gpm median yield, and estimated finished-well costs of $15,000-$25,800.
h1: What Portland, Colorado Well Records Tell Buyers
intro_html:
Buying land near Portland means understanding the local well records before you rely on a driller’s estimate. Within 5 miles of Portland in Ouray County, Colorado DWR records list 316 permitted wells. Of those, 189 are recorded as constructed, 196 report total depth, 70 report pump yield, and 25 report static water level.

Most permits identify household or domestic use, and most wells draw from unnamed fractured bedrock. That combination can produce usable water, but conditions can change sharply from one lot to the next. Nearby records are useful for planning, not a guarantee for a new well.

sections.heading: Portland well depths depend on fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Portland is 138 feet. The middle half runs from 77 to 263 feet, so a bid based only on the median may be too low or too high for a particular parcel. The 90th percentile is 495 feet, and the deepest record reaches 4,421 feet.

Depths are spread across the area: 35% of reported wells are under 100 feet, 42% are between 100 and 300 feet, 17% fall between 300 and 600 feet, and 6% are deeper than 600 feet. Permits most often name unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, including granite and gneiss conditions where water follows fractures rather than a uniform layer.

sections.heading: Portland well yields are usually workable, but not uniform
sections.html:
Among the 70 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 5.6 to 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a generally useful production range for a household well, but the spread matters when sizing storage, pumps, and a future home.

Only 3% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Another 13% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 53% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 31% report more than 15 gallons per minute. A low-yield well may still work with storage, but it deserves a specific pump and tank plan before construction.

sections.heading: Static water levels near Portland vary across the slope
sections.html:
The 25 reported static water levels have a median depth to water of 60 feet. The middle half extends from 8 to 144 feet. That range is wide enough to affect pump selection, well design, trenching, and the cost of bringing water to a building site.

The permit series does not show a simple decade-by-decade water-level trend. It does show continuing drilling activity: permits were issued in every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year being 2025. A static level from a neighboring well is useful local evidence, but it should not be treated as a guaranteed water level on another lot.

sections.heading: Permit history shows steady drilling around Portland
sections.html:
Domestic and household permits make up 75% of the recorded use mix. Stock wells account for 15%, irrigation for 6%, and monitoring for 10%. That pattern fits a mountain area where many parcels depend on individual wells rather than a broad municipal supply.

The most active drillers in the records are Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth), with 60 wells; Mccracken Well Drilling Inc (Mccracken, Alan E.), with 31; and Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.), with 11. These records can help identify local experience, but the current driller should still review access, geology, casing, grout, and the intended use before pricing the work.

sections.heading: Portland well drilling cost starts with the rock
sections.html:
For Portland’s fractured mountain bedrock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 138-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $9,000 to $13,800. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $15,000 to $25,800 at the median depth. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, or a low-yield result can change the final price. Ask for a bid that separates drilling from completion equipment and site work, rather than comparing a per-foot number alone.

sections.heading: Check water quality, mine history, and building constraints
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 555 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those records do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test before purchase and to ask how the site relates to mines, drainage, and known environmental areas.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock even when nearby wells produce well. Before building, confirm the permit’s allowed use, test the water, and plan separation between the well, septic system, and structures. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for the proposed use. Colorado DWR permit records should be checked alongside county building and septic requirements.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying a Portland lot
sections.html:
Start with wells closest to the parcel, then compare depths, reported yields, and static water levels rather than relying on a countywide average. Records near Ouray, 4 miles away, and Ridgway, 6 miles away, can provide context, but the local fractured-rock pattern makes the immediate neighborhood more useful than a distant comparison.

For a purchase, make water availability and quality part of due diligence. Have a licensed driller review access and likely depth, request a complete cost range, and preserve enough room for the well, septic system, driveway, and house site. For a new build, design around the actual well yield and storage plan. A domestic exempt well has a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and its permit conditions still control the allowed use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Portland, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Portland is 138 feet, with the middle half from 77 to 263 feet. Depths vary widely in the fractured mountain bedrock: 35% are under 100 feet, while 6% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 4,421 feet, so a nearby well is useful but not predictive by itself.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Portland, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 138-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $9,000 to $13,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $15,000 to $25,800. Difficult access, greater depth, or a low-yield result can increase the final cost.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Portland, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.6 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Reported results are mixed: 3% are under 1 gallon per minute, 13% produce 1 to 5, and 31% produce more than 15. Storage may help a low-yield household well, but it must be designed for the actual test result.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Portland, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield alone. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 555 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well before purchase and after construction, and review nearby mine and cleanup information with the appropriate local agencies.

faq.q: Are Portland, Colorado wells getting deeper or running dry?
faq.a: The available permit records do not establish a simple decade-by-decade water-level decline. Only 25 wells report static water level, with a median depth to water of 60 feet and a middle half from 8 to 144 feet. Fractured-bedrock wells can vary sharply between nearby parcels, so check neighboring records and obtain a site-specific driller’s opinion.
